expectedText:
CONFIDENTIAL MARRIAGE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

RECITALS — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This Confidential Marriage — Information Sheet is prepared in connection with Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan's interest in California's confidential marriage license, a distinct license track from the standard public marriage license issued under Family Code Part 2 (commencing with Section 350). This document is informational only. It records facts and statutory citations about the confidential-marriage track generally; it does not itself apply for or issue a marriage license, does not solemnize a marriage, and states no conclusion about whether a confidential marriage license is available to, or the better choice for, Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan specifically.

ELIGIBILITY — LIVING TOGETHER AS SPOUSES
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that, under California law, the confidential-marriage track is available only where two unmarried people, neither of whom is a minor, have been living together as spouses; a couple who meets that condition may be married under the confidential-marriage chapter by a person authorized to solemnize a marriage under the same statute (Family Code Part 3, Chapter 1, commencing with Section 400) that authorizes solemnization of a standard public marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "When two unmarried people, not minors, have been living together as spouses, they may be married pursuant to this chapter by a person authorized to solemnize a marriage under Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 400) of Part 3."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 500 (California Legislative Information text), the confidential-marriage eligibility condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=500.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code § 500); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the substantive eligibility condition for California's confidential-marriage track specifically — not a claim about which state's law, if any, governs a specific couple's situation, about whether any other state offers a comparable confidential license, or about how "living together as spouses" is defined or proven for this purpose (the statute itself does not define the phrase).

HOW A CONFIDENTIAL MARRIAGE LICENSE IS ISSUED — COUNTY CLERK OR AN APPROVED NOTARY PUBLIC
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that, except in a limited physical-inability circumstance addressed elsewhere in the statute, a confidential marriage license is issued by the county clerk upon the personal appearance together of both parties and payment of the required statutory fees. California law separately allows the county clerk to issue a confidential marriage license at the request of a notary public whom the county clerk has approved to issue confidential marriage licenses, upon that notary public's payment of the same statutory fees; the parties then reimburse the notary public for the fee amount.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Except as provided in Section 502, a confidential marriage license shall be issued by the county clerk upon the personal appearance together of the parties to be married and their payment of the fees required by Sections 26840.1 and 26840.8 of the Government Code and any fee imposed pursuant to the authorization of Section 26840.3 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 501(a) (California Legislative Information text), issuance by the county clerk on personal appearance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=501.)
  "The county clerk shall issue a confidential marriage license upon the request of a notary public approved by the county clerk to issue confidential marriage licenses pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 530) and upon payment by the notary public of the fees specified in Sections 26840.1 and 26840.8 of the Government Code. The parties shall reimburse a notary public who issues a confidential marriage license for the amount of the fees."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 503 (California Legislative Information text), issuance through an approved notary public (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=503.)
  Known gap: This draws on two different statutory sections within the same statutory Part (Family Code §§ 501(a) and 503); each was independently verified against the leginfo text. Both are one state's statutes, used as real evidence that a confidential-marriage license can be issued either directly by a county official or through a specially approved private notary public — a two-track issuance mechanism this project has not found stated for California's standard public marriage license. Not a claim about how any other state, if it has a comparable confidential-license category, structures issuance, nor about the physical-inability exception in § 502, which is not quoted here.

APPROVAL AND TRAINING REQUIRED BEFORE A NOTARY PUBLIC MAY ISSUE CONFIDENTIAL MARRIAGE LICENSES
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that a notary public may not issue a confidential marriage license unless first approved to do so by the county clerk, that approval requires the notary public to complete a county-clerk-conducted course of instruction on issuing confidential marriage licenses not exceeding six hours in duration, and that an approval, once granted, is valid for one year and must be renewed to continue issuing confidential marriage licenses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "No notary public shall issue a confidential marriage license pursuant to this part unless the notary public is approved by the county clerk to issue confidential marriage licenses pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 530(a) (California Legislative Information text), the approval requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=530.)
  "No approval, or renewal of the approval, shall be granted pursuant to this chapter unless the notary public shows evidence of successful completion of a course of instruction concerning the issuance of confidential marriage licenses that was conducted by the county clerk in the county of registration. The course of instruction shall not exceed six hours in duration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 532 (California Legislative Information text), the required course of instruction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=532.)
  "An approval to issue confidential marriage licenses pursuant to this chapter is valid for one year."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 533 (California Legislative Information text), the one-year validity of an approval (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=533.)
  Known gap: This draws on three different statutory sections within the same statutory Part (Family Code §§ 530(a), 532, and 533); each was independently verified against the leginfo text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a licensing and training regime for a private official (a notary public) issuing a category of marriage license can exist under state law — not a claim that any other state authorizes a notary public to issue any category of marriage license, or a statement of the renewal fee or the misdemeanor penalty for an unapproved notary's issuance, which this clause does not quote.

NO WITNESS-SIGNATURE REQUIREMENT STATED FOR THE CONFIDENTIAL-MARRIAGE CEREMONY
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that, for a standard public marriage license, California law requires the person solemnizing the marriage to enter on the license the printed name, signature, and mailing address of at least one, and no more than two, witnesses to the ceremony. The parallel statute governing a confidential marriage license after the ceremony — requiring only that the license be presented to the person solemnizing the marriage, that the solemnization section be completed, and that the license be returned to the county clerk within 10 days — states no witness-signature requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(d) The person solemnizing the marriage shall complete the solemnization sections on the marriage license, and shall cause to be entered on the marriage license the printed name, signature, and mailing address of at least one, and no more than two, witnesses to the marriage ceremony."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 359(d) (California Legislative Information text), the witness-signature requirement for a standard marriage license (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=359.)
  "(a) The confidential marriage license shall be presented to the person solemnizing the marriage.(b) Upon performance of the ceremony, the solemnization section on the confidential marriage license shall be completed by the person solemnizing the marriage.(c) The confidential marriage license shall be returned by the person solemnizing the marriage to the office of the county clerk in the county in which the license was issued within 10 days after the ceremony."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 506 (California Legislative Information text), completion and return of a confidential marriage license, with no witness-signature requirement stated (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=506.)
  Known gap: This compares two different statutory sections in two different Parts of the Family Code (§ 359, governing the standard public marriage license, and § 506, governing a confidential marriage license after the ceremony); each was independently verified against the leginfo text. The absence of a witness-signature requirement in § 506 is drawn from that section's silence on the point, set against § 359(d)'s explicit requirement — this project found no Family Code provision in the confidential-marriage chapter (§§ 500-511) that affirmatively states witnesses are not required, so this clause is limited to the textual contrast actually verified rather than that broader affirmative claim.

THE CONFIDENTIAL MARRIAGE RECORD IS NOT OPEN TO PUBLIC INSPECTION
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that, under California law, the county clerk maintains a confidential marriage certificate as a permanent record that is not open to public inspection except upon a court order issued on a showing of good cause, and that a confidential marriage license itself is a confidential record not open to public inspection without a court order. The county clerk may search for a confidential marriage certificate to confirm that a marriage exists, but the date of the marriage and any other information in the certificate may not be disclosed except upon court order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the county clerk shall maintain confidential marriage certificates filed pursuant to Section 506 as permanent records which shall not be open to public inspection except upon order of the court issued upon a showing of good cause. The confidential marriage license is a confidential record and not open to public inspection without an order from the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text), the confidential, not-publicly-inspectable record (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=511.)
  "The county clerk may conduct a search for a confidential marriage certificate for the purpose of confirming the existence of a marriage, but the date of the marriage and any other information contained in the certificate shall not be disclosed except upon order of the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 511(c) (California Legislative Information text), the limited existence-confirmation search (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=511.)
  Known gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions (a) and (c) of the same statutory section, Family Code § 511; this is a single statutory section, and no additional independent source was found for it. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a confidential, non-public records track for a marriage license and certificate can exist alongside a standard, more publicly accessible marriage record — not a claim about how any other state, if it offers a comparable confidential-marriage category, handles public access to those records, and not a claim about what "good cause" means or how a court order under this section is obtained.

WHO MAY OBTAIN A CERTIFIED COPY OF THE CONFIDENTIAL MARRIAGE CERTIFICATE
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that California law allows a party to a confidential marriage to obtain a certified copy of the confidential marriage certificate from the county clerk of the county where the certificate is filed, by submitting an application meeting the requirements set for certified copies of vital records under the Health and Safety Code, and upon payment of the fee equivalent to that charged for copies of a standard marriage certificate. The statute describes this certified-copy path as available to the parties to the marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A party to a confidential marriage may obtain a certified copy of the confidential marriage certificate from the county clerk of the county in which the certificate is filed by submitting an application that satisfies the requirements of Chapter 14 (commencing with Section 103525) of Part 1 of Division 102 of the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 509(a) (California Legislative Information text), a party's right to obtain a certified copy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=509.)
  "Copies of a confidential marriage certificate may be issued to the parties to the marriage upon payment of the fee equivalent to that charged for copies of a marriage certificate."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 509(b) (California Legislative Information text), the fee for a certified copy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=509.)
  Known gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same statutory section, Family Code § 509; this is a single statutory section, and no additional independent source was found for it. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a confidential-marriage record system can still make a certified copy available to the married parties themselves despite the record's general non-public status — not a claim about the exact Health and Safety Code application requirements referenced in § 509(a) (Chapter 14, commencing with § 103525), which were not independently verified here, nor a claim about whether anyone other than a party to the marriage may obtain a certified copy through this specific provision.

SIGNATURES AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan acknowledge review of this Confidential Marriage — Information Sheet on September 3, 2026, prepared with reference to the confidential-marriage provisions of the Alameda County county clerk's office and the California Family Code sections cited above.

Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

Taylor Morgan: ☐ _________________________

This information sheet is not a confidential marriage license application. An actual application must be completed on the form prescribed by the applicable county clerk.
